beats: Algorithms are either useful (BFS) or beautiful (Towers of Hanoi)
The FFT is both: it powers wireless and GPS, and it's gorgeous
Usually taught with heavy prerequisites; here a discovery approach via polynomial multiplication
Task: design an efficient algorithm to multiply two polynomials
The distributive law you learned in algebra is the naive algorithm
Coefficient list representation, index k holds the degree-k coefficient
Every term times every term: O(d^2); can we do better?
Simplest case: a line; what other representations map one-to-one to a line?
Two points fix a line; d+1 points fix a degree-d polynomial
Proof sketch with a system of equations and an invertible matrix; full proof linked
Multiply two concrete polynomials by multiplying 5 point values pairwise: O(d)
Grand plan: evaluate, multiply pointwise, convert back; the missing magic box is the FFT
Evaluate at n random points: back to O(d^2)
Simplify to x^2 at 8 points: which points let one value give another?
Positive-negative pairs: even functions repeat, odd ones flip sign
Split a general polynomial into even and odd parts, functions of x^2
Each half is another evaluation problem at half the points; smells recursive
Big picture: an O(n log n) recursive algorithm, if it works
One major problem: can you spot it? Squared points are all positive, so recursion breaks
Fix: extend the domain to complex numbers
Reverse-engineer with n=4: pick 1, then need x with x^2 = -1, which is i
Alternate view: we solved x^4 = 1, the fourth roots of unity
Degree 5 needs 8 points: eighth roots of unity; general rule for n
Roots on the unit circle written compactly as powers of omega = e^(2 pi i/n)
Two key properties: pairs, and squaring gives n/2 roots that are also paired
Full FFT outline: base case, two recursive calls, combine with omega^j
This part is tricky; take your time verifying each step
Translates the outline into 11 lines of code
Missing piece: interpolation, which seems much harder
Evaluation as matrix-vector product; the DFT matrix
What stands out about the inverse matrix? Omega becomes omega^-1 over n (skipping proofs)
So the inverse FFT is the same code with one line changed
Recaps the four brilliant ideas; why it is his favorite algorithm
